description_en: Cābahā Phalcā is part of a small cluster ofphalcāsaround Cābahā Bahi (14th cent. CE). They are still used forbhajanachantings and leisure activities. Situated at the southern edge of the street that leads to Okubahāl (east) from Tangaḥ and to the west of Cābahā Bahi (a monastic building dating back to the 14th cent. CE), the Cābāhāḥ Phalcā has had a dynamic history of destruction and reconstruction. An image of Umāmaheśvara was installed in 1680 AD, and thephalcāwas renovated on the same occasion, just 12 years after its initial construction. It collapsed during the 1934 Great Earthquake, and there is no evidence that it was reconstructed until the late 20th century CE. In 2002 it was finally reconstructed with the support of URBAN MANAGEMENT AND ECONOMIC DIVERSIFICATION PROJECT (UMEDP), the Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust (KVPT) and Jyapu Samaj in Lalitpur. It completely collapsed again during the 2015 earthquakes and in 2019 was once more rebuilt from the plinth up. The community undertook this work with funding from the municipality. Part of the reason that it took so long for thephalcāto be reconstructed was that the residential house attached to the rear of thephalcāalso needed to be rebuilt simultaneously. Moreover, financial resources were scarce in the wake of the earthquakes.The reconstruction process saw the reuse of four of the historical columns, though new ones were also introduced. These newer ones are somewhat too high and of rather low craftsmanship (Malaysian wood was used because the price for Salwood went up dramatically in the wake of the earthquakes).It is believed that Cābāhāḥ Phalcā was originally commissioned by a Shrestha family living in the adjacent rear house. On the basis of the pillars, the KVPT dated the structure back to the late 18th century in their Final Report of 2003, though they note that the columns may not have originally come from the arcaded rest house. An inscription in front of Cābahā Phalcā claims that it was initially constructed in 1668 CE. After the 1934 earthquake, six of the historic pillars were salvaged and stored, as well as the plinth base stones. The old brick foundation was visible for a long time, as well as some niches holding statues of deities. These deities have since been stolen, most probably some time in the 1980s.The safeguarding of threatened architectural heritage of the Valley was already a prominent issue in the early 2000s, and the reconstruction of this monument was part of a larger project that saw the restoration of 15 monuments deemed to be under threat due to urban encroachment and development. A contemporary report states that "[t]he reconstruction of thepāṭīto its original state portrays a model attempt to preserve the historic architectural type of rest house, and retains the significance of thepāṭīand its open space for the modern community. The project also involved the training of Nepalese team in project management, restoration project design, community negotiation, publicity and financial reporting." (Joshi and Ranjitkar Final Report Chabaha Pati 2003, p. 3) The report also stressed that these historic rest houses play a central role in Patan's World Heritage Site.Thephalcāis of great importance for the local Tamrakar community, and most of thebhajanamembers that regularly perform in the building come from this community. However, there is also a friendly relationship with the neighbouring Lũchẽ Nani Phalcā (LAL4100); the two groups help each other out and play music together.The Caturvyūha Caityā in front of thephalcāis an important resource; its inscription mentions the renovation of thephalcā,and an image of the building has been engraved into it. There is also a well in front of the structure.
description_ne: ओकुबहालबाट तङ्गः जाने बटोको दक्षिणी किनारमा, बालकुमारी मन्दिरको सामुन्ने रहेको चाबाहाः फल्चा विगतका ठूला भूकम्पको अनुभव सँगालेर उभिएको जस्तो देखिन्छ । सन् १९३४ को महाभूकम्पमा यो पूर्ण ध्वस्त भएको थियो । त्यसपछि सन् २००२ मा मात्र यसको केभिपिटि एवं अन्यको प्रयासमा पुनर्निर्माण भयो । त्यसपछि फेरि सन् २०१५ को भूकम्पमा यो पूर्णरूपमा ध्वस्त भयो । अहिले महानगरपालिकाको आर्थिक सहयोगमा स्थानीय समुदायद्वारा यसको पुनर्निर्माण सम्पन्न गरिएको छ । त्यस क्रममा चारवटा ऐतिहासिक स्तम्भहरूको पुनः प्रयोग गरिएको छ । स्थानीय ताम्राकार समुदायका मानिसहरू फल्चामा भजनगायन गर्ने गर्दछन् ।यस फल्चामा प्रयोग भएका काष्ठस्तम्भहरूलाई केभिपिटिको प्रतिवेदन २००३ मा १८ औं शताब्दीको मानिएको छ तर ती काष्ठस्तम्भहरू फल्चाकै नभएर अन्य कुनै ऐतिहासिक संरचनाको स्तम्भलाई यसमा प्रयोग गरिएको पनि हुन सक्छ । चभा फल्चाको अगाडि रहेको एउटा अभिलेखमा यस फल्चाको निर्माण सन् १६६८ मा भएको थियो भन्ने कुराको सङ्केत पाइन्छ । फल्चाको ठीक पछाडि घर भएका श्रेष्ठ परिवारले यो फल्चा स्थापना गरेका थिए भन्ने कुरामा स्थानीयहरू विश्वास गर्दछन् । सन् १९३४ को भूकम्पपछि फल्चाका छ वटा काष्ठस्तम्भ र पेटीका जगका ढुङ्गालाई सुरक्षित राखिएको थियो । त्यसपछि लामो समयसम्म जगका केही ईंटाहरू र प्रतिमास्थानमा रहेका देवताका मूर्ति मात्र धेरै वर्षसम्म फल्चाको अवशेषको रूपमा रहेका थिए, त्यसमा पनि सन् १९८० तिर देवताका मूर्तिहरूको चोरी भयो ।फल्चाको अगाडि एउटा इनार र एउटा चतुर्व्यूह चैत्य रहेको छ । यो फल्चाको पुनर्निर्माणसम्बन्धी अभिलेख यसै चैत्यमा टाँसिएको छ । त्यस अभिलेखमा सन् १६८० मा उमामहेश्वरको मूर्ति स्थापना गरिएको बताइएको छ । यसबाट निर्माण भएको १२ वर्षपछि ती मूर्तिहरू फल्चामा राखिएको देखिन्छ ।

historical_events.event_description: Cābāhāḥ Phalcā collapsed completely in the 2015 earthquakes. Musical instruments, books and statues of deities were all buried under the rubble. The traditional drums stored on the upper floor were later recovered by locals and had suffered some damages. However, a local Maharjan resident tells us that the images of Umāmaheśvaraand some other deities remained buried under the rubble, along with an inscription installed in the Phalcā.

The Cābāhāḥ Phalcā was restored on the basis of a plan designed by the Urban Management and Economic Diversification Project (UMEDP), the Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust (KVPT) and Jyāpu Samāja, Lalitpur. The final report was written up by Rohit Ranjitkar and Lumanti Joshi in March 2003.Six weeks of research went into the reconstruction process, where researchers tried to work out what the Cābāhāḥ Phalcā may once have looked like (its earlier forms had not been documented). Four different options for the front facade were developed and then shared with the community elders, who were ultimately responsible for the final decision. The window designs were copied from similarphalcādating back to the same period in the Chochhe Gallī area.Emphasis was given to the use of traditional building materials and craftsmanship, something which was uncommon back then.The reconstruction was also an attempt to challenge common views that traditional materials are not sustainable; those who argue this often propose cement be used instead. The process also included training workshops for and by traditional craftsmanship. Two new pillars were recarved on the basis of the historical model. Because it was in such bad shape, a layer of bricks adjacent to the residential house to the west was removed and replaced withma apāusing yellow mud mortar. The niches were installed in line with the photographs taken prior to the dismantling of the rear wall, and the stone statues of the guardian deities Gaṇeśa, Lokeśvara Kumāra, Umāmaheśvara and two others of Cābahā Phalcā were stored there. These statues have been carved anew. Some innovative measures were also introduced, such as putting a waterproof membrane between the planks and the mud bed for the roof tiles.
Donated by Harirāma Bhāvo and his wife Dhavaṃti from thenani(apparently, the courtyard is now known as Lũchẽ Nani) to the east of Jyāthabāhāra Vihāra.

historical_events.event_name: Renovation of the Phalcā and installation of a statue
historical_events.event_description: An inscription on thecaityain front of the Phalcā mentions that the Cābāhāḥ Phalcā was renovated and a statue of Umāmaheśvara was installed. The inscription names Harinandana Duvāra Bhāro as the donor of this and other properties in the name of hisīṣṭa devatā. It is likely that he also sponsored the construction of the Caitya and the renovation of the Phalcā, as well as the installation of the statue of Umāmaheśvara.The term 'bhāro'clearly suggests that Harinandana is from the Shrestha community. The extent to which the Phalcā was renovated is not clear. It is worth noting that the renovation was carried out just 12 years after its construction.
Cābāhāḥ Phalcā was finally reconstructed, though it remained a ruin from 2015 until 18 CE. The reconstruction was funded by local donors and the municipality.
